messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: estimating parameters of gaussian process
parts:
Hi,

Can somebody suggest how to speed up the estimation of GP parameters? In the code below I am using Squared Exponential kernel with one discrete variable arch (coded as 0 or 1) and two continuous variables (wavelength & bandwidth). I wonder if using Cholesky will help.  Or any other tricks? Sorry for two many spaces in the code...

Thanks,
Linas

data {
    int <lower = 0> N;
    vector [N] response;
    vector [N] arch;
    vector [N] wavelength;
    vector [N] bandwidth;
}
transformed data {
}
parameters {
    real <lower = 0> sigmaf;
    real <lower = 0> sigman;
    real <lower = 0> l;
    vector [8] c;
}
model {
    matrix [N, N] Sigma;
    vector [N] mu;

    // off-diagonal elements
    for (i in 1 : (N - 1)) {
        for (j in i : N) {
            Sigma [i, j] <- sigmaf * exp (-(pow (arch [i] - arch [j], 2) +
                pow (wavelength [i] - wavelength [j], 2) +
                pow (bandwidth [i] - bandwidth [j], 2)) / (2 * l));
            Sigma [j, i] <- Sigma [i, j];
        }
    }
    // diagonal elements
    for (i in 1 : N)
        Sigma [i, i] <- sigmaf + sigman; // + jitter
    // priors
    sigman ~ cauchy (0, 2.5);
    sigmaf ~ cauchy (0, 2.5);
    l ~ cauchy (0, 2.5);
    c ~ normal (0, 100);

    for (i in 1 : N) mu [i] <- c [1] +
        c [2] * arch [i] +
        c [3] * wavelength [i] +
        c [4] * bandwidth [i] +
        c [5] * arch [i] * wavelength [i] +
        c [6] * arch [i] * bandwidth [i] +
        c [7] * wavelength [i] * bandwidth [i] +
        c [8] * arch [i] * wavelength [i] * bandwidth [i];
    response ~ multi_normal (mu, Sigma);
}

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating parameters of gaussian process
parts:
You can pre-compute all the distances in transformed parameters.

It seems that student_t(4,0,2.5) is being recommended these days over cauchy(0,2.5) as the former is relatively heavy-tailed but not so much so that it causes computational issues like the former.

That normal(0,100) prior is probably slowing you down; is there a way to rescale the inputs so you can have a normal(0,1)? Besides, while I'm relatively new to GPs, this is the first time I've seen a GP with a non-zero prior on the mean; normally c would be set in transformed data as a vector of zeros.

The cholesky form shown in the manual should definitely improve ess/time.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating parameters of gaussian process
parts:
Precomputing the distances can certainly help, but because the 
covariance matrix depends on the parameters you have to compute
it at every iteration and there won’t be much benefit to computing
the Cholesky decomposition yourself (the multi_normal does a
Cholesky behind the scenes).  

There are some weak nonidentifiabilites in these kernels that we’ve
been debating, but the difference between that student_t and the
Cauchy will still be relatively small.  Similarly, having a non-zero
mean function shouldn’t cause too much trouble.

The immediate concern, however, is the discrete “arch” variable.
Trying to model a discrete covariate like that with a GP is typically
a bad idea.  Ultimately the more you cover the range of covariate
values the better identified your GP will be (and the better it will
fit), and with only 0 and 1 you’re not really constraining the hyperparameters
all that much.

It seems that student_t(4,0,2.5) is being recommended these days over cauchy(0,2.5) as the former is relatively heavy-tailed but not so much so that it causes computational issues like the former.

That normal(0,100) prior is probably slowing you down; is there a way to rescale the inputs so you can have a normal(0,1)? Besides, while I'm relatively new to GPs, this is the first time I've seen a GP with a non-zero prior on the mean; normally c would be set in transformed data as a vector of zeros.

The cholesky form shown in the manual should definitely improve ess/time.

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating parameters of gaussian process
parts: For the discrete parameter issue, could you maybe model the data as the sum of two latent GPs, where one GP forms the intercept and the other forms the arch effect (- this Gap for arch level 0, - this GP arch level 1)?

On Tuesday, 12 July 2016, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thanks a lot.

Are there any tricks to constrain hyperparameters? Maybe use GPstuff for initial estimates and then switch to rstan?

Linas

On Tue, Jul 12, 2016 at 2:31 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
Precomputing the distances can certainly help, but because the 
covariance matrix depends on the parameters you have to compute
it at every iteration and there won’t be much benefit to computing
the Cholesky decomposition yourself (the multi_normal does a
Cholesky behind the scenes).  

There are some weak nonidentifiabilites in these kernels that we’ve
been debating, but the difference between that student_t and the
Cauchy will still be relatively small.  Similarly, having a non-zero
mean function shouldn’t cause too much trouble.

The immediate concern, however, is the discrete “arch” variable.
Trying to model a discrete covariate like that with a GP is typically
a bad idea.  Ultimately the more you cover the range of covariate
values the better identified your GP will be (and the better it will
fit), and with only 0 and 1 you’re not really constraining the hyperparameters
all that much.

On Jul 12, 2016, at 6:58 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:

You can pre-compute all the distances in transformed parameters.

It seems that student_t(4,0,2.5) is being recommended these days over cauchy(0,2.5) as the former is relatively heavy-tailed but not so much so that it causes computational issues like the former.

That normal(0,100) prior is probably slowing you down; is there a way to rescale the inputs so you can have a normal(0,1)? Besides, while I'm relatively new to GPs, this is the first time I've seen a GP with a non-zero prior on the mean; normally c would be set in transformed data as a vector of zeros.

The cholesky form shown in the manual should definitely improve ess/time.


On Tue, Jul 12, 2016 at 2:16 PM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi,

Can somebody suggest how to speed up the estimation of GP parameters? In the code below I am using Squared Exponential kernel with one discrete variable arch (coded as 0 or 1) and two continuous variables (wavelength & bandwidth). I wonder if using Cholesky will help.  Or any other tricks? Sorry for two many spaces in the code...

Thanks,
Linas

data {
    int <lower = 0> N;
    vector [N] response;
    vector [N] arch;
    vector [N] wavelength;
    vector [N] bandwidth;
}
transformed data {
}
parameters {
    real <lower = 0> sigmaf;
    real <lower = 0> sigman;
    real <lower = 0> l;
    vector [8] c;
}
model {
    matrix [N, N] Sigma;
    vector [N] mu;

    // off-diagonal elements
    for (i in 1 : (N - 1)) {
        for (j in i : N) {
            Sigma [i, j] <- sigmaf * exp (-(pow (arch [i] - arch [j], 2) +
                pow (wavelength [i] - wavelength [j], 2) +
                pow (bandwidth [i] - bandwidth [j], 2)) / (2 * l));
            Sigma [j, i] <- Sigma [i, j];
        }
    }
    // diagonal elements
    for (i in 1 : N)
        Sigma [i, i] <- sigmaf + sigman; // + jitter
    // priors
    sigman ~ cauchy (0, 2.5);
    sigmaf ~ cauchy (0, 2.5);
    l ~ cauchy (0, 2.5);
    c ~ normal (0, 100);

    for (i in 1 : N) mu [i] <- c [1] +
        c [2] * arch [i] +
        c [3] * wavelength [i] +
        c [4] * bandwidth [i] +
        c [5] * arch [i] * wavelength [i] +
        c [6] * arch [i] * bandwidth [i] +
        c [7] * wavelength [i] * bandwidth [i] +
        c [8] * arch [i] * wavelength [i] * bandwidth [i];
    response ~ multi_normal (mu, Sigma);
}

}

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating parameters of gaussian process
parts: Current Stan is slow for GPs due to big autodiff expression tree for covariance matrix operations, There is work in progress to implement internal covariance function which whould provide significant speed-up. The priors and mean functions doesn't have much effect on the speed, and Linas's code is otherwise fine except it would be better to use separate l for each covariate. Half-Cauchy prior can make HMC/NUTS slower as the covariance function parameters are weakly identified and the posterior is then likely to have a thivk tail, but changing half-Cauchy to something with less thick tail is not going to make this much faster.

On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 9:31:15 PM UTC+3, Michael Betancourt wrote:
The immediate concern, however, is the discrete “arch” variable.
Trying to model a discrete covariate like that with a GP is typically
a bad idea.

And I think one of the great properties is of GPs is that how easy it is to build hierarchical models by using discrete covariates! I've never had problems when combining discrete and continuous covariates.  The Linas's model above already does automatically the sum of two latent GPs, that Mike proposes :)

Ultimately the more you cover the range of covariate
values the better identified your GP will be (and the better it will
fit), and with only 0 and 1 you’re not really constraining the hyperparameters
all that much.

For a single binary covariate the covariance matrix collapses to 2x2 covariance matrix. If exponentiated quadratic (aka squared exponential) is used it has two degrees of freedoms. I think this covariance matrix would be in many cases well identified and thus also the corresponding discerete GP ie normal distribution would be well identified, although there is dependency between sigmaf and l (and sigman) making them not so well identified. What I try to say is that you don't need to worry so much about the identifiability of hyperparameters and even less in discrete case :)
 
Aki

In the degenerate 2x2 case the two parameters should be identifiable
(the variances constraining the marginal variance, the covariances
constraining the product of the marginal variance and length scale)
but they will still be nonlinearly correlated and without sufficient data
they can still be hard to fit!  At least in the world of _finite_ data.  ;-)

parts: For the variable that is continuous but you only measured it at 2 levels, I don't believe that there's any benefit in treating it as a second continuous dimension in the GP; indeed, it may even be computationally wasteful. My understanding is that with only 2 measurement points, you'll only ever find support for at max a linear effect anyway. So, really you have a single-dimension GP measured at 6 points crossed with two 2-level discrete variables.
